title: 2 Kings 3:13–27
context: Elisha rebukes Jehoram and agrees to inquire only out of regard for Jehoshaphat. With a musician playing, the LORD’s hand comes on him, and he announces water without wind or rain and victory over Moab. The water arrives at the time of the morning sacrifice; the Moabites, seeing it red in the sunlight, mistake it for blood, rush the camp, and are routed. The campaign devastates Moab until the siege of Kir Hareseth, a Moabite stronghold the passage does not describe further. The chapter ends with the king of Moab offering his oldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, an act of child sacrifice that the law condemns (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10). The narrator then reports great wrath against Israel and Israel’s withdrawal without explaining the source or meaning of that wrath, and interpreters differ on it. Both traditions affirm the LORD’s provision of water and the victories as his work, and both read the ending as sober and unresolved rather than as approval of what the king of Moab did.

verses.text: Elisha said to the king of Israel, “What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father, and to the prophets of your mother.” The king of Israel said to him, “No, for the LORD has called these three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha rebukes Jehoram sharply, sending him to the prophets of his father and mother, a pointed reference to the prophets Ahab and Jezebel had favored. Arminian readers see a call to repentance in this rebuke, since it exposes the king’s divided loyalties and invites him to recognize where true prophetic authority lies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the prophet will not flatter a king who has trusted false prophets, and they note that Jehoram’s reply again blames the LORD without any sign of repentance. Both traditions agree that the verse shows Elisha’s independence from royal power and his faithfulness to the LORD over political convenience.

verses.text: Elisha said, “As the LORD of Armies lives, before whom I stand, surely, were it not that I respect the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward you, nor see you.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha swears by the LORD of Armies, before whom he stands, and says he answers only out of respect for Jehoshaphat. Arminian readers note that the faithfulness of one king brings blessing to others in his company, and that God’s mercy in this crisis is shaped by the presence of a believer among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the regard for Jehoshaphat as an instance of God’s covenant mercy toward David’s line, which extends benefit to those joined to it. Both traditions agree that Elisha’s oath reflects his conscious service in the presence of the LORD, and that the deliverance to come is undeserved by Jehoram.

verses.text: But now bring me a musician.” When the musician played, the LORD’s hand came on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha asks for a musician, and as the musician plays the LORD’s hand comes on him, recalling the link between music and prophecy in 1 Samuel 10:5. Arminian readers note that the prophet prepares himself to receive the word, showing human readiness and divine initiative working together in this moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the word comes only when the LORD’s hand comes on Elisha, underscoring that prophecy is God’s gift and not a technique. Both traditions agree that music here serves as a setting for receiving revelation, and that the text does not explain the precise relationship between the music and the coming of the LORD’s hand.

verses.text: He said, “The LORD says, ‘Make this valley full of trenches.’
verses.arminianNotes: The command to fill the valley with trenches calls for practical obedience before any water appears. Arminian readers see this as a summons to act in faith, since digging trenches in a dry valley only makes sense if the promise is trusted, and the soldiers’ labor is a real response to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God prescribes the means as well as the end, so that the trenches are part of how the LORD has determined to provide. Both traditions agree that the command honors human labor while making clear that the source of the water will be God alone, not the effort of those who dig.

verses.text: For the LORD says, ‘You will not see wind, neither will you see rain, yet that valley will be filled with water, and you will drink, both you and your livestock and your other animals.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises water without visible wind or rain, so that people and animals may drink. Arminian readers note God’s care for the needs of the whole army, livestock included, and they stress that the promise invites trust precisely because it cannot be explained by the ordinary signs of coming rain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the promise a display of God’s sovereign power over creation, providing without the usual means. Both traditions agree that the water in the desert is shared ground: God meets real need, his word is reliable, and his provision does not depend on what human eyes can see coming.

verses.text: This is an easy thing in the LORD’s sight. He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls the provision of water an easy thing and adds a promise of victory over Moab. Arminian readers note that God’s generosity exceeds what the kings asked, and some observe that the later outcome, including Israel’s withdrawal, invites careful reflection on how the promise was fulfilled in the events that followed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that nothing is hard for the LORD and that the promise of victory is fulfilled in the rout of Moab described in the following verses. Both traditions agree that the Moabites are indeed delivered into the kings’ hand in battle, while interpreters differ on how the abrupt end of the campaign relates to the scope of this promise.

verses.text: You shall strike every fortified city and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree, and stop all springs of water, and mar every good piece of land with stones.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The oracle describes a devastating campaign against Moab’s cities, trees, springs, and fields. Arminian readers note that this is presented as what will happen, and some observe that it sits uneasily with the restraint on cutting down fruit trees during a siege (Deuteronomy 20:19–20), a tension interpreters handle in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also notice the severity of the campaign and read it within the setting of judgment on a rebellious vassal in a particular historical moment. Both traditions agree that the verse should be read soberly as an account of ancient warfare, and that interpreters differ on whether it functions as a command, a prediction, or both, and on how it relates to Deuteronomy 20.

verses.text: In the morning, about the time of offering the sacrifice, behold, water came by the way of Edom, and the country was filled with water.
verses.arminianNotes: The water arrives in the morning about the time of offering the sacrifice, linking the provision with Israel’s worship. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to his promise, and they note that the trenches dug in obedience now receive the water the LORD said he would send.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight that the water came by the way of Edom at the appointed hour, displaying God’s precise timing and his rule over creation. Both traditions agree that the narrator presents this as the LORD’s doing, and while some readers suggest distant rainfall as the means, the text emphasizes divine provision rather than explanation.

verses.text: Now when all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, they gathered themselves together, all who were able to put on armor, young and old, and stood on the border.
verses.arminianNotes: The Moabites gather everyone able to put on armor, young and old, and stand at the border. Arminian readers note that Moab responds with its full strength to defend its land, and that the narrator treats the Moabites as real actors making their own decisions in the conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Moab’s mobilization only sets the stage for the outcome the LORD has already announced through Elisha. Both traditions agree that the verse shows the seriousness of the conflict and that the story is moving toward a confrontation in which God’s word will be fulfilled.

verses.text: They rose up early in the morning, and the sun shone on the water, and the Moabites saw the water opposite them as red as blood.
verses.arminianNotes: In the early morning sun, the Moabites see the water opposite them as red as blood. Arminian readers note that the text attributes the appearance to the sun shining on the water, and that the Moabites’ interpretation flows from what they expected to see rather than from what was actually there.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using the very water he provided for Israel as the means of Moab’s confusion, so that a single act of provision serves both deliverance and judgment. Both traditions agree that the narrator does not explain the color beyond the sunlight, and they avoid speculating beyond what the passage states.

verses.text: They said, “This is blood. The kings are surely destroyed, and they have struck each other. Now therefore, Moab, to the plunder!”
verses.arminianNotes: The Moabites conclude that the kings have destroyed one another and rush to plunder. Arminian readers note how quickly a mistaken assumption leads to reckless action, and they draw a sober lesson about acting on appearances without discernment or counsel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Moab’s miscalculation God’s power to frustrate the plans of his people’s enemies, as in other stories where confusion overtakes Israel’s foes (Judges 7:22; 2 Chronicles 20:22–23). Both traditions agree that the verse shows human misjudgment serving the outcome the LORD had promised.

verses.text: When they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and struck the Moabites, so that they fled before them; and they went forward into the land attacking the Moabites.
verses.arminianNotes: When the Moabites reach the camp, the Israelites rise up, rout them, and advance into the land. Arminian readers note that God’s promised victory comes through the army’s real engagement in battle, and that divine provision and human action work together in the outcome without competing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the victory fulfills the word spoken through Elisha in verse 18, showing that the LORD’s promise determines the result. Both traditions agree that the victory is the LORD’s gift, received through the fighting of the kings’ forces, and that the narrator credits the outcome to God’s word.

verses.text: They beat down the cities; and on every good piece of land each man cast his stone, and filled it. They also stopped all the springs of water and cut down all the good trees, until in Kir Hareseth all they left was its stones; however the men armed with slings went around it and attacked it.
verses.arminianNotes: The campaign proceeds as the oracle described, until only Kir Hareseth remains, surrounded and attacked by slingers. Arminian readers note the thoroughness of the devastation and observe that the narrative records the cost of war on land and people without glorifying it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the correspondence between verse 19 and verse 25 as evidence that God’s word is fulfilled in detail. Both traditions agree that Kir Hareseth is presented as Moab’s last stronghold in this campaign, that the passage gives no further description of it, and that the siege brings the war to its crisis.

verses.text: When the king of Moab saw that the battle was too severe for him, he took with him seven hundred men who drew a sword, to break through to the king of Edom; but they could not.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Moab attempts a desperate breakout with seven hundred swordsmen toward the king of Edom, but fails. Arminian readers note the narrative’s attention to a ruler driven to the edge, and they see the humanity of the enemy kept in view even in defeat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that every human escape fails when God has determined the course of a battle, and they see Moab’s failure as part of the fulfillment of the oracle. Both traditions agree that the text does not explain why he aimed at the king of Edom, and they refrain from supplying a motive the narrator does not give.

verses.text: Then he took his oldest son who would have reigned in his place, and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. There was great wrath against Israel; and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Moab offers his oldest son, the heir to his throne, as a burnt offering on the wall: an act of child sacrifice that Scripture elsewhere condemns (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). Arminian readers note that the narrator then reports great wrath against Israel without explaining its source, and they hold the possible readings, such as the LORD’s displeasure with Israel or a surge of hostility against Israel, with appropriate tentativeness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the sacrifice as a grievous act and hold that, whatever the great wrath was, the LORD alone is God. Both traditions agree that the meaning of the wrath is debated and that the text does not settle it, recording only that Israel withdrew and returned to its own land, which leaves readers with a sober and unresolved ending.
